headline: Medium prompt-injection and data-leakage risk from shared filesystem and editor-buffer exchange; Copilot’s GitHub-backed context adds compliance exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue can read/write workspace files and use MCP, while Copilot reads repo context and open buffers. That creates a plausible default pathway where malicious content in shared files or buffers can influence the other agent’s instructions. The pair lacks provenance tracking in the profiles, so uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace directory
IF either agent treats file contents as trusted instructions
mitigations: Separate the agents into different workspaces
Disable MCP servers for Continue during Copilot sessions
Review shared files before opening them in either agent
Use a read-only clone for one agent
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents read source code and open buffers, so sensitive code can flow into both contexts by default. Continue also has broad network egress and handles model-provider API keys, while Copilot sends context to api.githubcopilot.com. The shared workspace plus outbound context transmission makes leakage plausible in default use.
conditions: IF the shared workspace contains secrets or regulated code
IF either agent is used on the same files without redaction
mitigations: Remove secrets from the workspace before use
Use separate repos for sensitive and non-sensitive work
Turn off networked assistance for one agent on secret-bearing files
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately
requires-engineering: enforce secret scanning before context upload

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Continue can write filesystem state and shares state via filesystem across IDE windows; Copilot can write filesystem and modify git state. Even though Copilot’s shared-state claim is limited, both agents can mutate the same repo, so concurrent edits and git conflicts are plausible in default configurations. The uncertainty around orchestration locking warrants medium.
conditions: IF both agents edit the same repository concurrently
IF git operations occur without external locking
mitigations: Assign only one agent write access at a time
Pause one agent before the other applies edits
Commit or stash changes after each agent turn
Use separate branches per agent
requires-engineering: add file-level locking in the orchestrator

D_cascading_error.rationale: Copilot Workspace can propose and apply edits, and Continue can emit tool-assisted suggestions via MCP. If one agent’s output is fed into the other without verification, errors can cascade into incorrect code changes or actions. The profiles do not show a mandatory verification gate between them, so the interaction is a default medium risk.
conditions: IF one agent’s generated code or plan is pasted into the other agent
IF the receiving agent applies edits without human review
mitigations: Require human review before applying any suggested edit
Ask each agent to cite the source of claims in its output
Compare both agents’ diffs before merging
Use one agent only for drafting and the other only for review
requires-engineering: add automated verification of agent-generated changes

E_compliance.rationale: Continue is open-source and locally oriented, but Copilot is closed-source and sends context to GitHub’s API with a GitHub repo OAuth scope. That creates a compliance mismatch for data residency and retention-sensitive code, especially if regulated data is present. The profiles do not prove a specific violation, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated or residency-bound data is opened in Copilot
IF organizational policy forbids sending repo context to GitHub
mitigations: Exclude regulated files from Copilot sessions
Use a local-only assistant for residency-bound work
Review vendor retention settings before use
Limit Copilot access to non-sensitive repositories
requires-engineering: document a data-processing agreement and retention policy
